title: Respirable crystalline silica: where it comes from and why it matters
audience: All stone and terrazzo restoration workers, leading hands and supervisors, including people who only assist on site
learningOutcomes: Describe how respirable crystalline silica is released from stone and terrazzo work
List the dust-generating processes in stone restoration, including honing and polishing
Explain why dry work, dry sweeping and compressed air are stop-work matters
Explain why respiratory protection is the last control, not the first
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: Safe Work Australia, Working with silica and silica containing products (national guidance) (February 2022); NT WorkSafe, Guide to working with crystalline silica and crystalline silica containing products (v1.1) (version 1.1, 29 January 2026); WorkSafe Victoria, Working with engineered stone (reviewed 27/08/2024); NSW, Position paper: regulatory approach to crystalline silica regulation (April 2025).

instruction.heading: What silica dust is and how it is released
instruction.body: Crystalline silica is a mineral that occurs naturally in many rocks and sands, and it is present in many stones, aggregates and some terrazzo mixes. When these materials are cut, drilled, ground, sanded, sawn or polished, very fine particles can be released into the air. The particles that matter for health are respirable, which means small enough to reach deep in the lungs. Crushing, cutting, drilling, grinding, sanding, sawing and polishing all appear in the national guidance (February 2022) as dust-generating work. For this course, the processes that matter most are honing, grinding, polishing and any dry cutting or dry sweeping that follows them. The national guidance names silicosis, progressive massive fibrosis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chronic bronchitis and lung cancer as health effects of exposure, and also mentions chronic kidney disease and autoimmune disorders.

instruction.heading: Why dry work is the stop-work case
instruction.body: The NT WorkSafe guide (version 1.1, 29 January 2026) says dry cutting, grinding or polishing without on-tool extraction, water suppression or local exhaust ventilation generates very high levels of respirable crystalline silica. The national guidance rules out compressed air, dry sweeping and general-purpose vacuums for cleaning surfaces and clothing, because they spread the dust into the air. Honing and polishing are wet processes in this course, and they are only safe when the water is running at the point of cut and the slurry is controlled. A task that starts dry, that loses its water feed partway through, or that is cleaned up with dry methods has moved outside the course's safe methods. Stop the task, make the controls work, and record the stop. Do not carry on because the job is nearly finished.

instruction.heading: Plan before the first pass
instruction.body: Before work starts, list each task that will create dust. Name the control for each task: a wet method, on-tool extraction, local exhaust ventilation or isolation of the area. Check that the control is available and working before the first pass, not after the first dust cloud. In occupied buildings, such as offices or cafes, plan the isolation of the area as well, so that other people are kept away from the work. Victoria's guidance calls for a written silica hazard control statement, which has to exist before high-risk work begins. If any listed control is not available, the work does not start that day.

procedure: Do not start if the material is not identified.
List every task that will cut, grind, hone, polish, sand, saw or drill the surface, and note which ones are dry or could become dry.
For each task, name the control to be used: a wet method with water at the point of cut, on-tool extraction, local exhaust ventilation, or isolation of the area.
Check that the water feed, extraction and isolation are ready before the first pass.

Confirm the cleaning method you will use at the end of each task, and confirm that it is a wet method, low-pressure water or a rated vacuum as stated in “Dust controls: wet methods, extraction, isolation and housekeeping”.
Confirm that respiratory protection is planned as the last control, and that the fit test requirement in “Respirators, fit testing and health monitoring” is met.
If any control is missing, or a task would become dry, stop, record the stop and tell the supervisor.

workedExamples.situation: A restorer is booked to hone a terrazzo floor in an occupied office on a Monday morning. The site has no water tap near the work area. The client says the dust is fine and asks the restorer to open the windows and wear a dust mask.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the correct decision, and what is the first control to set up?
workedExamples.reasoning: Opening windows and a dust mask do not make dry honing safe. A wet method is the main control, and the site has no water supply. The office is occupied, so isolation is also needed. The correct decision is to stop, reschedule or arrange a water supply and an isolated area before any honing, and to record the reason. Respiratory protection is planned after the engineering controls, not used instead of them.

equipmentAndPpe: Water supply and feed for wet honing or polishing, confirmed before start
On-tool extraction or local exhaust ventilation suited to the task (see “Dust controls: wet methods, extraction, isolation and housekeeping”)
Barriers, signs and isolation materials for the work area
Respiratory protection planned per “Respirators, fit testing and health monitoring” (fit tested before use)
Site PPE set by the site induction

commonErrors.error: Assuming dust is only a problem when it can be seen.
commonErrors.prevention: Respirable particles are generally not visible. Put the controls in place before the work starts.

commonErrors.error: Dry sweeping after honing to save time.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a wet method for cleaning, as set in “Dust controls: wet methods, extraction, isolation and housekeeping”. Dry sweeping is stop-work.

commonErrors.error: Relying on a dust mask as the main control.
commonErrors.prevention: Respiratory protection is the least effective control. Engineering controls come first and PPE is never the only control.

commonErrors.error: Starting a dry task because the water feed is far away.
commonErrors.prevention: Arrange the water feed or change the job plan before starting. Do not work dry.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Victoria's guidance treats every engineered stone process as high-risk crystalline silica work. Duties differ by state.

Stop-work rule: stop immediately if any dust-generating task is dry, if the wet method or extraction stops working, if the area is not isolated when it should be, or if a required control plan or hazard statement is missing. Make the control work or change the plan, and record the stop before resuming.

The national guidance (February 2022) lists health effects of exposure, including silicosis and lung cancer; use that list and no other medical claims in client or staff material. This lesson does not grant silica authority or any licence.

qualityStandard: Every dust-generating task is listed before the first pass.
A named control is set up and checked for each task before work starts.
No dry dust-generating task proceeds at any point.
Any stop is recorded with the reason and the corrective action.
documentationEvidence: Task list showing each dust-generating process
Control chosen for each task, with a check record
Isolation and signage record for occupied areas
Stop-work record with reason and corrective action
summary: Honing, grinding, polishing, cutting, drilling and sanding can release respirable crystalline silica.
Respirable dust is generally not visible, so controls go in before work starts.
Dry work, dry sweeping and compressed air are stop-work matters.
Engineering controls come before respiratory protection.
Missing controls mean the work stops until they are in place.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which process is named as dust-generating for silica-containing products in the 2022 Safe Work Australia guidance?
options: Wiping with a damp cloth to lift the film
Applying a sealer by brush to the surface
Grinding, sanding, sawing and polishing
Rinsing with low-pressure water over the stone

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about silica dust is correct?
options: It is only dangerous when it is visible in the air around the work area and the whole site today
It is a risk for outdoor work only, away from the house, the rooms, the workshop and the sheds
It is removed by normal domestic vacuuming after the work is done and the room is aired out today
Respirable particles are generally not visible, so controls must be in place before work starts

knowledgeChecks.question: Which cleaning method is named in the NT WorkSafe guide as one that must not be used on silica dust?
options: Compressed air
Water spray jet
Wet sweeping
M-class vacuum

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement about respiratory protective equipment is correct?
options: It is the first and most effective control to use on the job site today
It is the least effective control and must never be the only control
It replaces wet methods on short jobs and quick tasks at the site today
It is needed only for outdoor work on the roof and the yard areas at the site

knowledgeChecks.question: Terrazzo contains aggregate. What does this mean for the course?
options: Terrazzo is always silica-free, so no controls are needed at all on the job
Terrazzo is an engineered stone and must not be touched at all by the crew
Terrazzo is treated as silica-containing until its composition is known
Terrazzo needs silica controls only when it is cut or drilled on the job
